title: The thicker the horn, the greater its spiral curvature

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The thicker the horn, the greater its spiral curvature

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: On the whole, thicker horns are more strongly spirally curved than slender ones, because a larger cross-section allows greater differences in growth or retardation between opposite sides.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I think it may be said that, on the whole, the thicker the horn, the greater is its spiral curvature.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XIII, “The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion”; topic “Summary of horn growth”. Scope: horns of antelopes, goats and sheep

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch13-08: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.80

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The comparative association is directly measurable with standard morphometrics. Public 3D collections can provide a substantial sample, though the proposed causal explanation is less directly tested.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure horn cross-sectional thickness and centerline curvature in a taxonomically broad 3D sample, then model their association with controls for body size, sex, age and phylogeny. A robust positive effect supports the claim; a null or negative effect with adequate power refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
External scans may not reveal sheath thickness separately from the core.

Thickness and curvature both covary with body size and age.

fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.82

operationalizability: 0.94
data existence: 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Thickness and curvature are ordinary measurements on horns that are already scanned or photographed, and a phylogenetic regression is standard. The open sample can test the tendency in the better-represented bovids and is not a balanced survey of every antelope. Shared ancestry can produce the same association Thompson attributes to the room a thick cross-section gives for unequal growth, so the geometric correlation is more resolvable than that mechanical reason.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Regress a curvature or spiral-tightness measure on basal horn diameter across antelopes, goats, and sheep, with a phylogenetic control. The claim is supported by a positive thickness–curvature relationship within and across clades; no relationship, or the reverse, would refute the stated tendency.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Related species share both thick horns and strong spirals, so a naive correlation is phylogenetically confounded.

Scanned samples under-represent slender-horned antelopes relative to sheep and goats.
